title: The Price of Victory
theme: The representation of victory through military glory, captivity, wounded bodies, civilian vulnerability and mourning.
ordering: Historical sequence by the represented original work or composition; captions distinguish the dates of later casts and replicas.
interpretation: Comparisons of different cultural and political uses of war imagery, without claiming direct influence or a continuous historical progression.

works.title: Lying Wounded Warrior from the Temple of Aphaia
works.caption: c. 500–490 BCE. A warrior lies wounded in a figure from the west pediment of the Temple of Aphaia. Isolated from the larger composition, his vulnerable body becomes the center of attention. The exhibition begins here, before a victor is named: what does fighting do to the people whose bodies make a battle possible? This model records a later plaster cast.

works.title: Roman Soldiers Attacking, from Trajan's Column (Scene CXV)
works.caption: 113 CE. Roman soldiers attack in a relief from Trajan’s Column, a monument celebrating the emperor’s campaigns in Dacia. Military violence becomes part of a public account of imperial achievement. Compare the troops with the wounded warrior: a collective image of strength can give a different meaning to combat than a single injured body. Atrium shows a scan of a plaster cast.

works.title: Vessel with Battle Scene
works.caption: 600–900. Prisoners stripped of their battle regalia are brought before a Maya lord, contrasting with the elaborately dressed warriors. This cacao vessel probably circulated as a political gift. Victory becomes something to display and exchange: the captives’ humiliation helps establish the authority of the people who commissioned, gave, or received it.

works.title: Plaster Cast of a section of the bas-relief of Bayon depicting a Naval Battle
works.caption: 12th–13th-century Khmer relief; plaster cast made in 1904. At Bayon, a naval battle enters the carved narrative of a temple. Compare its setting with Trajan’s column: warfare can become part of the enduring image of a society’s power. This cast carries only a section of that larger account. The surrounding architecture, other scenes and original setting shape how such a battle is read.

works.title: The Dying Tecumseh
works.caption: Modeled c. 1837–1846; carved 1856. Tecumseh led an Indigenous coalition against U.S. expansion. Decades after his death, Pettrich imagined him as a fallen classical hero. The Smithsonian identifies this as a fictive portrait and questions its presentation of conquest as inevitable. A defeated leader can be given a noble image while the continuing significance of his resistance is pushed aside.

works.title: Mourning Victory Melvin Memorial
works.caption: Memorial designed 1906–1908; this marble replica carved 1912–1915. Victory raises a flag and laurel, yet lowers her eyes. French designed the memorial for James Melvin, whose three brothers died in the American Civil War. Triumph and bereavement occupy the same figure. Can a monument honor a victory without making loss seem worth its price?

works.title: Stop War
works.caption: 2022. A girl has fled in her nightclothes and tries to protect her teddy bear. Fenriz describes the sculpture as a tribute to children and other civilians caught in war. The person doing the protecting also needs protection. After armies, captives and monuments, this small act changes the measure of courage—and asks whose safety a victory is meant to secure.
